source.title: SaaS: Speed as a Supervisor for Semi-supervised Learning
source.authors: Safa Cicek; Alhussein Fawzi; Stefano Soatto

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Measures how label corruption changes training-loss reduction speed on ResNet18, bearing on V2, but does not measure time to fit labels or reproduce the original training-error measure.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports training-loss curves and loss after 10 epochs for five label-corruption levels. The text states that loss decreases more slowly as the percentage of correct labels decreases. The paper's statement that deep networks can fit random labels is attributed to cited work [12], so it is not recorded as this study's result.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 directly tests V2's corruption-dependent slowing using ResNet18 training-loss curves and loss after ten epochs. It does not measure time to perfect fitting or the constant-factor overhead of random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that early training speed depends strongly on label correctness and use this dependence to estimate unknown-label distributions before supervised weight training. SaaS improves over labeled-only baselines and achieves competitive semi-supervised benchmark performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies label corruption and measures training loss over a short interval; it does not report the original random-label fitting and training-error experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss curves vary with label-corruption fraction. Figure 1 uses a fixed learning rate of 0.1 with no data augmentation or weight decay.
record.problems: The claim-relevant Figure 1 results are figure-only in the supplied text, so exact values cannot be extracted. The study reports loss reduction over epochs, not training error or time to fit; no test error is reported for these conditions.

untested.parts: Own results establishing zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters. Eventual random-label fitting is attributed to Zhang et al.
Time required to fit true versus random labels completely, and whether the overhead is only a small constant factor.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fitting and steadily increasing test error across corruption fractions, including simultaneous signal learning and noise memorization.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting, and whether removing regularization preserves generalization on true labels. Figure 1's unregularized setup provides no such comparison.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise within training. Comparing aggregate loss curves across corruption levels does not establish that temporal ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The qualitative states rely on Figure 1's explicit caption, not reconstructed numerical values. SaaS performance and augmentation requirements do not establish results about random-label fitting or its regularization dependence.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report its own test of fitting completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, or whether architecture and hyperparameters remain unchanged.

The study reports training-loss speed across corruption levels, but not time to fit random labels, a small constant-factor time comparison, or a quantified convergence rate. Figure-only values are not reconstructed.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment is reported.

The study does not report training error and test error across label-corruption levels. Its training-loss curves do not establish perfect fitting, steadily rising test error, or capture of remaining signal.
No experiment tests whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms generalization on true labels.
No experiment compares when or how real versus random labels are learned over training.
